chapter: American Jazz Orchestra, conducting and teaching
title: American Jazz Orchestra with John Lewis
summary: The AJO at Cooper Union, its personnel, Central City Sketches with Benny Carter and Ellington recordings.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: We’ve been at this for quite a while, so we’re going to have to do Part Two, but I wanted to ask you about the Jazz Museum in Harlem. Did you have to interview for that position, and did you give them a philosophy, a pitch so to speak?

In the early 1990s I started to branch out a little bit more. I was involved with something called the American Jazz Orchestra, with John Lewis, that started in 1985, 1986. And this was a band comprised of mostly big band veterans: Marvin Stamm, Virgil Jones, John Eckert, Benny Powell, Jimmy Knepper, Eddie Bert, I think I said him, Danny Bank and Jerry Dodgion and Jerome Richardson and Bill Easley and Dick Katz and great bass players including we made a record with Ron Carter and Howard Collins on guitar. It was a great band. And we started doing concerts down at Cooper Union, and this was a chance where John Lewis who was an absolute idol of mine, as he would be for most anybody. Because I loved his piano playing so much. On top of everything else. And that band lasted about maybe eight years or so. Gary Giddins was the artistic director. And we made a series of recordings. Probably the best known one would be “Central City Sketches” with Benny Carter and this was when Benny, at the age of 79 or 80, came out of retirement and wrote a suite and recorded it and when it came out on an album it created quite a bit of buzz. It was a great record. “Central City Sketches.” Then we also recorded the music of Duke Ellington for Nesuhi Ertegun on Atlantic Records where I had to play all the Ben Webster things. And the music of Jimmy Lunceford and maybe one more record. So that took up a lot of my time.
